1. What I noticed is that the highest percentage of smokers comes from people with an income of <35k. I also noticed while looking at the graph that the more income one makes, the less the percentage of smoking is. 
2. I wonder as to why people with less income smoke more than those with higher incomes. I wonder this because if they have less income, wouldn’t they want to spend it more on things they need like food, water and their house? It makes me wonder if those of less income smoke more than those of higher incomes because of stress.

1. I noticed that people with a higher income tend to smoke less than people with a lower income, which shows an inverse variation between the 2 variables being measured. 21% of people who earn an income of < $35,000 smoke while only 7% of people who earn an income of > $100,000 smoke. I also wonder why people with lower income tend to smoke more even though they can likely not afford as much smoking materials as opposed to higher income households.
3. This could also have an impact because there would be an increased amount of deaths in the community, especially in essential workers in the lower income households, which could have an impact on the amount of essential workers there are in out society, affecting people of all incomes and backgrounds.
4. Headline: Smoking in the Lower Class Is On the Rise

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
By analyzing the graph, I noticed that people with lower household income tend to smoke more. On the other hand, as household income increases, the percentage of people who smoke reduces.

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder how the circumstances related to having low household incomes affects a person's likelihood to smoke. This population could be smoking to distract themselves from the hardships associated with having lower incomes. Additionally, populations with insufficient money may not be educated on the consequences of smoking cigarettes.

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
The impacts on smoking make several impacts to my community and society in general. Smoking directly causes deaths, which impacts families and communities around the world. The usage of nicotine in cigarettes can also cause personality changes and addiction. To prevent the impacts of smoking, assistance programs can be introduced to help people in need.

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline.
This graph displays the direct correlation between poverty and smoking rates throughout the world. A title which encompasses the idea of the graph could be "Smoking: The Demographic Disparity".

In fact, 21% of people that smoke “every day” or “some days” earn less than $35,000 per year in household income, while only 7% earn greater than $100,000 per year in household income. 1. I noticed that the majority of people who smoke more earn less than $35k.
2. I wonder why the people who earn less smoke more. Why are they using the little spending money they have on cigarettes?
3. This shows that smoking is more of a problem with people of lower incomes, because health may not be their number one priority. We can only so so much by telling people smoking is bad, but it's not that easy to stop if you have an addiction. If we raised the prices of cigarettes, more people would rather spend their money on necessities.
4. The graph is showing how common smoking is among people with lower incomes, and how willing they are to spend money on cigarettes. A headline for this graph could be, "Smoking vs. Income" or, "What is the relationship between smoking and income?"

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that people with higher incomes smoked less.
2. I wonder if the reason they smoke less is because they are more educated (and thus earn more money).
3. It means that if you are in a generally richer/more educated community, then you will find less people smoking. It also means that the habit of not smoking will be passed down from person to person meaning everyone will be safer (including me).
4. "Does a higher income mean less chance to smoke?"

raw_comment:
- What do you notice?

But there are some more low income communities in my area, who lean towards smoking. Smoking, just as proven by this data, can greatly, negatively affect you. So, it is very important to not smoke.
- Catchy Hook Title: How smoking takes over your income.

raw_comment:
Notice: 
I notice that as the household income increases, the percentage of people who smoke decreases. For example, in the graph it shows households that make less than $35K have a higher number of smokers compared to those who make more than $100K.

Wonder:
I wonder if the professions of the people in the household, and if there are other factors related to the income that causes stress, leading them to smoke.

Impact: 
After seeing this data, I think that it is important to be more aware about the problem of smoking that is more likely to happen when households have a lower income. 

Analyze + Heading:
In the graph, it shows that 21% of those who earn less than $35K smoke, and 7% of people who make more than $100K  smoke. I think that there is a relation between the household income and if a person smokes frequently. I would title it  Household Income effect on Smoking Habits.

Notice

I notice that as income decreases the amount of smokers increase. The income that smokes the most is <35k a year and the income level that smokes the least is >100k an year income. 

Wonder

I wonder why the amount of cigarettes decreases with wealth because normally you would assume that with more money you can buy more cigarettes. raw_comment:
1. With this graph I noticed that those under the highest income were around twice as likely to smoke compared to those with lower income. It shows that the people with the <35k income have one of the larger gaps from 35k-75k while 35k-75k and 75k-100k only have a 2% difference.
2. I wonder if the reason wealthy people are wealthier is because of their habits and self restraint, or if the reason why wealthy people have a smaller percentage is because of their environment in comparison to those with lower income. 4) "Is there a Correlation Between My Income and My Smoking Habits?"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
	I notice that there is a negative correlation between the percentage of people that smoke “every day” or “some days,” and household income. In fact, 21% of people that smoke “every day” or “some days” earn less than $35,000 per year in household income, while only 7% earn greater than $100,000 per year in household income. This shows a clear inverse relationship between household income and percentage of people that smoke “every day” or “some days.” Furthermore, I also noticed that at least 21% of people that smoke every day or some days earn less than the US median salaries per capita in 2020. 

What do you wonder?
           As we can tell in the graph, 21 + 15 + 13 + 7 is equal to 56, which in this case refers to 56%. This means that the graph only accounts for 56% of some surveyed population. I would wonder if the remaining 44% that was not represented on this graph would consist of all that do not smoke at all. In addition, although there is an inverse relationship between our two variables, though we obviously know that correlation is not always causation, I wonder if an increase in smoking is a defined cause of a decrease in salary.

4) In the graph we just see the comparison of income with the probability of smoking. I would put the title as How does income have an effect on a probable smoker.

raw_comment:
What impact does this have on you and your community?
        This graph would actually tend to provide valuable information on the impact of those that smoke regularly on various communities. We can infer that, because lower income households are generally more likely to smoke than higher income households, that lower income households will also be exposed to much higher levels of smoking deaths. As stated, in the first paragraph, “Cigarette smoking is responsible for more than 480,000 deaths per year in the United States.” By the same token, the opposite would be true as well - higher income households tend to have less chronic smokers, along with lower numbers of deaths attributable to cigarette smoking. It is also important to note that cigarettes typically contain nicotine, which is an addictive substance. This can add to even higher costs that lower income households are more likely to face.

What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the  graph’s main idea.
        I would say that this graph is portraying the relationship between household income and the percentage of smokers that smoke “every day” or “some days.” I would probably name this graph, “The Effect of Smoke on Money.”

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice looking at the graph that most "every day" smokers earn less than $35,000 in income. Few smokers earn more than $100,000 in income. The household incomes increased, while the smokers decreased. This shows throughout all income categories. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder how smoking seems to have such an impact on income earned. Smoking is a very expensive habit, I wonder why smokers wouldn't try hard to earn a high income. Did having a low income cause smokers to start smoking, or vice versa?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts my community because I can see, from looking at this graph, how impactful smoking can be on your household income. raw_comment: Somethings I noticed about this graph is that people who have low incomes smoke more than people with higher incomes. But this cannot conclude that smoking causes people to have lower income. The graph does show that the higher the income the lower the percentage of smokers. This makes me wonder why people with low incomes feel the need to smoke and what keeps people with higher incomes to not smoke. It also makes me wonder if environment plays a big role in smokers, if wealthier backgrounds contribute to not smoking. Maybe people who have less than 35k income use smoking to cope with the stress. Even though me and my community has never had to face these challenges, I imagine it's very hard to live in a low income community where not only is the air being contaminated by smokers but it's a very unhealthy way of living. This graph mainly shows that the higher the income the less people smoke. It's left leaning and makes me wonder if smoking is related to wages. If I had to write something catchy for the title, I would write " Does your income relate to the likeliness of buying a pack of cigarettes?".

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that in this graph, it shows how income can be proportionate to how likely people smoke. It shows incomes using groups from an income of less than 35k, 35k-75k,75k-100k, or more than 100k.
2. I wonder why a lower income may be a motivation or struggle that leads to smoking. I also wonder if the people who have a higher income smoke less because of their environment, and how they are not as exposed to smoking quite as much. It is quite a shock to learn how much adults in the US smoke, but even more how income can contribute to that.
3.  This impacts me by wanting to change these graphs by spreading more awareness to both my community, and the communities that have a higher percentage of smokers. 
4. Does lower income correlate to higher smoking rates?
That would be my graphs title/main idea.

raw_comment:
1. With this graph I noticed that those under the highest income were around twice as likely to smoke compared to those with lower income. It shows that the people with the <35k income have one of the larger gaps from 35k-75k while 35k-75k and 75k-100k only have a 2% difference.
2. I wonder if the reason wealthy people are wealthier is because of their habits and self restraint, or if the reason why wealthy people have a smaller percentage is because of their environment in comparison to those with lower income. I also wonder if the reason for the huge difference between 35k-75k and <35k is because it’s lower than the average income and they cope with the stress using cigarettes. 
3. While this doesn’t have a huge impact on me or my community, this definitely has an impact for others. Smoking can cause serious issues with lungs and the addiction will always be embedded in their brains. This is a real issue that can result in death. 
4. This graph is a bar graph, it uses categorical data to show the percentage for each wage group. It is a left leaning graph with the majority of smokers having lower wages. This graph makes me think about whether having lower wages is a cause for smoking or if smoking lead to lower income. If I had to come up with a catchy title I would say “Does Having Lower Income Lead to Being More Prone to Smoking?

raw_comment:

2. I wonder why people with less money would smoke more because smoking can be an expensive habit and they don't have as much money to waste.
3. This doesn't impact me because no one in my family smokes and I don't think any of our friends do either. But, I want my community to be as healthy as possible, so I'm glad we all have pretty well-off incomes.
4. This graph is showing us that wealthier people tend not to smoke as much as people with less money. I would say a title could be: Household Income vs. Smokers.

1. One thing I noticed was that the % of smokers were greater/more commonly found in lower income households, which holds true for all 4 data ranges.

This data leads me to believe that there is a trend/relationship with how much people make vs whether they smoke, and that trend is kept consistent throughout this whole graph.

raw_comment:
1.) While looking at this graph I noticed that as the income increased the number of smokers decreased. This shows us that the graph is skewed to the right.
2.) I wonder why people with lower income smoke more, even if they have less money? Does this mean that smoking is so addicting that it causes them to use up the little money they have on cigarettes?
3.) An impact this has on me is that this shows how addicting smoking can be. People with lower incomes are willing to sacrifice their money on cigarettes. We need to work together to help people stop their addiction and work to prevent people from smoking.
4.) This is a bar graph that uses percentage to show how much percent of people smoke based on their household income. The skew of this graph is right meaning that lower incomes smoke more. Along with that you can see a huge drop from <35k to 35k-75k with a change of 6%. Also there is a huge drop from 75k-100k to >100k with a change of 6%. This means that there is a big change when it comes to smokers with different incomes.

raw_comment:
1. One thing I noticed was that the % of smokers were greater/more commonly found in lower income households, which holds true for all 4 data ranges. 
2. I wonder why lower income households spend the limited money they have on cigarettes, and I wonder if the cause of their smoking habits started because they were making lower income, or vice versa.  
3. Although I am fortunate to have a family that provides all my needs for me, and to live in a more "well-off" community, I understand that other communities may have more people making less income.  I want my community to thrive with as large household incomes as possible, and to keep my community healthy by limiting the amount of smokers in it as much as possible.  
4. This graph shows how people who make less income are more likely to smoke "every day" or "some days" than people who make a higher income amount.  Although I'm sure there are some outliers in this graph(people who make a lower income but don't smoke or people who make a higher income but do smoke), the main thing I can conclude about this graph is that the more you make, the less likely you are to smoke. 21% of people who make less than $35k dollars smoke, 15% of people who make $35k-75k smoke, 13% of people who make $75k-100k smoke, and 7% of people who make more than $100k smoke.  This data leads me to believe that there is a trend/relationship with how much people make vs whether they smoke, and that trend is kept consistent throughout this whole graph.

raw_comment:
1. One thing I noticed was that the % of smokers were greater/more commonly found in lower income households, which holds true for all 4 data ranges. 
2. I wonder why lower income households spend the limited money they have on cigarettes, and I wonder if the cause of their smoking habits started because they were making lower income, or vice versa.  
3. Although I am fortunate to have a family that provides all my needs for me, and to live in a more "well-off" community, I understand that other communities may have more people making less income.  I want my community to thrive with as large household incomes as possible, and to keep my community healthy by limiting the amount of smokers in it as much as possible.  
4. This graph shows how people who make less income are more likely to smoke "every day" or "some days" than people who make a higher income amount.  Although I'm sure there are some outliers in this graph(people who make a lower income but don't smoke or people who make a higher income but do smoke), the main thing I can conclude about this graph is that the more you make, the less likely you are to smoke. 21% of people who make less than $35k dollars smoke, 15% of people who make $35k-75k smoke, 13% of people who make $75k-100k smoke, and 7% of people who make more than $100k smoke.  This data leads me to believe that there is a trend/relationship with how much people make vs whether they smoke, and that trend is kept consistent throughout this whole graph.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that people who tend to make less money smoke more than people who make more money. 
It can also be inferred that people who smoke more spend more money on cigarettes thus meaning they lose money. A pack-a-day habit results in $188 per month or $2,292 per year. This is a substantial amount of money. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why people who tend to make less money smoke more often. One theory is that people who make less have more financial problems in their lives and thus need a way to escape the stress. Nicotine, which is a sedative and a stimulant, allows people to escape briefly from reality and heightens their mood. People who make more money don't have as many stress factors which means they don't need to find ways to relax and escape. Another theory is that people who can't afford a better education like the one people with more money can get didn't receive much encouragement to not part take in drugs/smoking. However, this point is very subjective.

What impact does this have on you and your community?
This doesn't have a strong impact on me or my community. However, it does worry me that people smoke because it leads to more deaths which is bad. In addition, in theory, the more people there are who smoke the higher the chances of teens wanting to fit in or teens who are pressured into smoking by smokers. 

What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
When money is a means to an end.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that the graph is overall right-skewed, with the graph showing that the lower the income, the more the people in the sample smoke. This is very clear to see, as 21% of those who smoke make less than 35k, while only 7% of those who make more than 100k smoke. It is very easy to see that income and smoking are not independent of one another.
 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder if the geographical location has any sort of impact on the percentage of smokers. Maybe if someone lives in a more densely populated area, working an office building job is more likely to pick up smoking than someone living in a more rural area. 
 
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
I live in a state that is primarily middle and upper-class families, this issue still pertains to here. This impacts my community because it is sad to see those around me who do smoke not able to break this harmful addiction.
4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Smokers and their income

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
 
I noticed that there was a direct link between people who smoke and their income. A whopping 21% of people who either smoke every day or some days make less than $35,000 per year. On the other hand, only 7% of smokers make more than $100,000. I also noticed that as the annual income went up, the percentage of smokers went down.
 
2. What do you wonder?

raw_comment:
I notice a clear trend where the higher the income bracket you look at, the less percentage of the people in said bracket are smokers. For example, more than a fifth of the people in this statistic that make less than $35,000 annually are smokers, however, when looking at people that make more than $100,000, you would only see roughly 7/100 people being smokers.

I wonder how this statistic has changed over the years. Especially in the days before the consequences were known, it seemed like everybody smoked as if it was almost a sign of wealth. raw_comment:
I notice that there is a relationship between how much you make and the percentage of people that smoke. 21% of people who make less than $35k a year smoke, while only 7% of people who make more than $100k per year smoke. 
  I wonder why more people who make less money smoke more if they do not have the money to waste on smoking? I wonder if maybe they smoke to relieve the stress they have of having money issues? I also wonder if there was a graph of a wider range of drugs than just smokers what those graphs would look like. 
  This has an impact on my community because although I would say it is on the wealthier side, for the most part, there are still areas where people do not have too much money and might be smoking. This makes it even more for my community to continue to educate kids so that they do not fall into the trap of smoking. 
  This graph is showing that there is a relationship between income and smoking.
A catchy headline could be ¨Less money, more smoking¨

4.
“Wealth and Lung Health”

raw_comment:
I notice that people in lower income households tend to smoke more frequently than people in higher income households. For households that earn less than $35,000 yearly, more than twenty percent of people smoke. However, for households that earn more than $100,000 a year, less than 10 percent of people smoke.
I wonder why people of lower income households are more likely to smoke than higher income households. Is it because smoking is used as a coping mechanism?
It impacts my community because my town is split into upper-middle class households and low-income households. It is important to know how income affects the likelihood of smoking so, as a community, we can try to both prevent people from starting to smoke and help people quit smoking.
This graph illustrates the relationship between the percent of people who smoke and their annual household income.

raw_comment: I notice the lowest income bracket of <$35k has the highest rate of “every day” or “some days” smokers. Conversely, the highest income category has the lowest rate. Given the high cost of cigarettes, this inverse relationship between income and smoking seems counterintuitive. We can't assume a cause-effect relationship from this observational study, but it's fair to say that other factors might be involved to explain it. I wonder where this seeming correlation between smoking and income comes from. In part, could it be inferior health education in poorer communities regarding the repercussions of tobacco? Could it also be strategic advertising by manufacturers to target the poor population? If this is the case, is it unethical and worth government intervention? Coming from a mostly upper-middle-class city, this graph doesn't have a direct impact on the vast majority of us. However, given that about a fourth of NH citizens make less than $35k/year, this information is important to all of us. Smoking has many horrific health consequences, but those with lower incomes often don’t have health insurance. The health of our state’s economy could be negatively impacted by smoking-related morbidity. It’s important for us to be aware of the relationship between smoking and income as its cause may be unethical and preventable. The main idea of the graph is that there's an inverse relationship between smoking rates and annual income. Headline: "Income and Smoking, Could They Be Related?"

raw_comment:
“Smoking, the Killer of Lungs and Bank Accounts”

I notice that the lower the income, the more people smoke. Although most would assume that high income people would smoke more because they can afford to spend, but the graphical display shows that that is not in fact the case. In addition to this, it is also shown that people whose income is more than 100k smoke very much less more often than not. 

I wonder why smoking is still popular or even in question when it is well known that it is bad for you. I understand that a majority of the people who still smoke, especially in the U.S, are probably all people who have smoked for a long time and are now addicted.


As someone who lives in a predominately middle /upper class area, I don't think that this issue is as prevalent as the majority of those who do smoke here can afford it. However, the lower income/impoverished people in my town may be more likely to smoke or have smoked. This effects my community because of the immense damage can do to your health and overall well being. Smoking should be more regulated in public areas, especially in this time of safety and social distancing.

The main purpose of this graph is to show that people with a lower income are more likely to smoke than those with a higher income.

raw_comment:
I notice that there is a relationship between different income levels and percentages of people who smoke. The graph is right-skewed, with the highest percentage (21%) of smokers falling within the less than $35,000 household income bin and the lowest percentage (7%) of smokers falling within the over $100,000 bin.
I wonder why individuals with lower incomes have the highest rate of smoking? I wonder if the inclusion of other drugs, such as prescription medicines, would change the levels of usage among different income levels? While the over $100,000 bin may have the lowest levels of smoking, I wonder if it would have higher levels of prescription drug use due to potential insurance coverage? Also, I wonder if each block is dominated by a certain age group? The lower income levels may be dominated by younger people while the higher income levels may consist of older people. 
Members of my community that fall into lower income brackets may be more likely to smoke, which will most likely cause long-term health consequences. Since premature death and illness are caused by smoking, my community should focus on funding treatment options for people with addictions. These treatment options should be free to everyone to ensure that they are accessible to all income levels. 
The smoking and income graph shows that individuals with lower household incomes are at higher risk of smoking than individuals with higher household incomes.
“Is Income a Predictor of Smoking Levels?"

raw_comment:
The graph on the New York Times article is very simple and easy to read. The first thing I noticed when looking at the graph is that the highest percentage of smokers were grouped into the less than $35 thousand dollar annual revenue category. Along with that I noticed that as the annual income of people increased, the percentage of smokers decreased. I think this is interesting as the results of the graph show this trend to be very steady and consistent. From these findings, I am wondering if there are more smokers with smaller wages because money might be a problem for them. I know that many times people that smoke or are addicted to drugs originally started because they are going through a rough time in their life, and  felt they needed something to ease the pain. I wonder if the graph is showing the same thing, as more people are smoking to help them cope with possible money problems they are having.
	The findings in this graph might also be able to explain why there aren’t a ton of smokers all around our city. Our town is considered to be overall on the wealthier side, which would put us towards the middle of the graph shown. This would mean that we shouldn’t have a particularly higher percentage of smokers living in town, and I believe that to be true from my experiences growing up. A headline that this graph could be placed under is, “Smokers by Income”.

raw_comment:
I notice that household income has a clear influence on cigarette smoking.  Based on the display, the percentage of those who earn under $35k a year have a significantly higher smoking percentage compared to that of other annual earnings.  The percent of smokers for wage areas of $35k-75k is also similar to that of $75k-100k.  
I wonder why the percentage of $35k-75k is only 2% off from $75k-100k.  The difference between these two groups is much less than the others, as there is a 5% difference between smokers of >$100k and $75k-100k, and there is a 7% difference between smokers of <$35k and $35k-75k.
It’s good that, given information below the graph, smoking is on the decline around the country.  Due to a decline in smoking overall, the health of my family and others around me will be better, not only due to passive smoke-inhilation, but also family members who may smoke or have quit smoking.  
“Has low wages turned Americans to smoking?”

raw_comment:
I notice that there is a relationship between household income and whether adults smoke or not. The lowest level of household income of less than 35,000 dollars a year had the highest percentage of smokers at 21%. I noticed that this percentage gradually went down as income increased. I noticed that the highest income level of greater than 100,000 dollars had the lowest percentage of smokers at 7%. 
I wonder why people who have lower income tend to be more likely to smoke? I wonder if the financial struggles of those who make less money has any effect on whether or not people smoke cigarettes. I also wonder how much money people that have low income spend on cigarettes and how this plays in with their ability to make ends meet. 
This impacts me and my community because smoking is very dangerous and has detrimental effects on people every single day. As seen in the graph many people who have low income tend to smoke, this is an issue that affects my community and people across the world. It is important that my community is aware of this and can help to spread awareness on this issue. It is possible that people with low income have higher stress levels from financial struggles and use smoking as a way to cope with this. 
This graph shows various income brackets and the corresponding percentage of people who smoke. 
Title: “Smoking vs. Income level: A deadly battle”

raw_comment:
I notice how this graph is generally right-skewed, as the lower the income, the more the sample people smoke. As 21% of those who smoke make less than 35k annually, while only 7% of those who make 100k+ smoke. It's clear that income has a large effect on the likely hood that people smoke.

I wonder if not only income but also the geographical location has a large impact on the percent of people who smoke. For example, maybe someone who lives in rural Maine and makes >35k a year is less likely to pick up smoking than someone who lives in a large city.

Although I live in a region of my state which generally middle class and upwards, we can still face problems with smokers within the lower-income bracket. Despite not being around a lot of smoking, on a state level, New Hampshire struggles. It's sad to hear this after knowing how much funding has gone into the extensive research behind cigarettes and how they are harmful.

The graph from this article details the relationship between the annual income salary of smokers within the United States. MY headline would be: “Does wealth dictate addiction?”

raw_comment:
1) I notice that the rate of smoking among people who make >$100k is significantly lower than that for people who make <$35k. In general: the lower the income category, the higher the rate of smoking.
2) I wonder why this is the case. I don’t think there is a cause-effect relationship here, and certainly this is not caused by some moral failing of the poor. Are sociological factors common to smokers also common to people having less income? Is it the fact that old, retired people are more likely to smoke and also more likely to be in the <$35 category?
Also, this graph only analyzes smoking, (tobacco, I presume). What about other drugs? Alcohol? Cannabis? Etc.
3) I live in a relatively wealthy area, so for most people in my community this won’t be that much of a problem. But we have to be conscious of the health concerns of EVERYONE in our community. Take COVID-19. It’s a respiratory disease, so being a chronic smoker is not very good during these times. Lacking adequate health insurance or medical care is also not very good during a pandemic. Both of these problems are correlated to being low income, so we have to be cognizant of the fact that this disease will disproportionately affect the poor. And now people are making less money due to the economic devastation during the pandemic, exacerbating this problem.
4) The main idea of this graph is that people in lower income categories are at a higher risk of smoking. My headline would be “Does Being Poor Mean Smoking More?”

The data shows that 21% of people smoking are making less than $35k annually, and it also shows that only 7% of the smoking population make over $100k annually. As annual income increases, the percentage of smokers decreases. 
 
I wonder if these numbers have changed significantly or not in the past ten or twenty years. I know anxiety is actively present in our world today, so does mental health play a role in an individual's income whether they smoke or not? 
 
This impacts my community because I see people smoking daily, which has a negative impact on their health and can be deadly in the long run. It also has an impact because the people around me who have a lower income, are more likely to smoke, which is dangerous for their health.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
 
After observing the graph, I noticed what appears to be a clear correlation between income and smoking. Those in the lower class appear to smoke consistently more than their upper-class compatriots. I also notice that the largest decreases in percentages are from the <35,000 and the >100,000 or the two extremes. 
 
2. What do you wonder?
 
I wonder if the correlation in smoking goes beyond income. I also wonder what steps can be taken to minimize smoking in lower-income households. What steps have not been tried yet that could work to minimize this number?
 
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
 
This impacts myself and my community as it shows a clear problem that exists in this country and in communities nearby. If these problems go unattended, thousands in my own community and state could develop smoking-related diseases and become sick. Not only could these people suffer but also their families as “addiction is a family disease, one person may use, but the whole family suffers.” 
 
4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
 
This graph depicts the correlation between yearly household income and the percentage of those who smoke. The graph is broken down into four categories based upon income and shows a clear correlation between income and the percentage of those who smoke. A possible catchy headline could be, “Poverty Strikes Again”

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the map:  “More Wealth, More Health” by Jade of New York, "Smoke and Money" by Mrs. D’Angelo’s 5th grade class from Elmhurst, Illinois, "Who's Lighting Up?" by Hannah of Iowa, and “Going Up in Smoke: The Relationship Between Household Income and Smoking” by Libby of New Hampshire.
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, March 5 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston and Tonya Adkins of Charlotte, North Carolina, neither of whom smoke, but this does not affect our incomes or v.v.

raw_comment: I noticed that there is a trend of those who earn less income smoking more. Approximately 21% of those who earn less than $35k annually, the lowest income bracket, smoke often, compared to 7% of those who earn over $100k annually, the highest income bracket. This graph suggests there is a relationship, whether causational or not, between household income and the percentage of smokers. As income increases, the percentage of smokers decreases. I wonder if this is true because smoking for many is used as a coping mechanism. Since those in lower-income brackets tend to deal with more stress related to finance, are the percentages of smokers higher for this reason? I also wonder what a map would look like which shows the states and their average income and percentage of smokers. I think this data would be interesting to see as it would allow us to compare data state-by-state as opposed to just generalized data. This information impacts my community as it shows those around me who earn less have a higher tendency to smoke and are therefore putting themselves at risk for many health issues. However, I am very fortunate to live in a wealthy part of the U.S., which means according to this graph not many people smoke. I would be able to back this up as I do not see many people in my community smoking. This graph shows income brackets and their corresponding percentage of smokers. My alternate title for this graph is "Going up in Smoke: How Income May Be Affecting the Smoking Rate".

raw_comment:
The main thing I noticed was that the percentage of smokers decreases as income increases. This shows us that income could 
be a factor in who smokes and who doesn’t. 
 
I wonder why people with less money tend to smoke more? Why would they spend their money on cigarettes? Although this is a generalization, maybe stress levels (due to lower-income) could contribute to the large population of smokers at a low-income level. I made this inference because I know that some people use smoking as a stress reliever. 

This impacts me and my community, as smoking is an unhealthy habit that could have long-term effects on people’s health. As I mentioned before, this could be an indicator of the stress levels based on income level. Another study would need to be conducted to prove this point. 
Headline: “Is Smoking Dictated by Income Level?”

raw_comment:
I notice that the percentage of smokers who smoke “every day” or “some days” is higher at lower incomes. The largest percentage of smokers, 21%, is recorded at an income of 35,000 dollars. As the income increases, the percentage of smokers decreases. The smallest percentage of smokers, 7% is recorded at an income of 100,000 dollars. There is a relationship between smoking and a person’s income. 
I wonder why there is a decrease in the percentage of smokers when the income increases. It would be interesting to conduct this same survey from another country and compare their results to the United States’. I wonder if the results from a country like Canada or Mexico would show the same relationship between smoking and a person’s income. In the United States, more people smoke when receiving a lower income. 
Smoking impacts my community in a negative way. It is an unhealthy habit that is causing serious health problems. The percentage of smokers who smoke “every day” or “some days” is higher at lower incomes. These people could be spending their money on many other things. This data has revealed a great number of people who smoke. As a community, we should try o find a solution to decrease the number of smokers who receive a lower income. 
Increase The Income, Decrease The Smoking

I notice that there is a direct correlation between the percentage of people who smoke every day and household income. Those who smoke every day are more likely to have a household income below $35k than those who do not smoke every day. Only 7% of people who smoke every day make over $100k annually, while 21% of people who smoke every day make under $35k.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the correlation between smoking and income exists? What is it about a person that smokes that makes it more common for them to have a lower household income? 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
Whenever I go to New York City, the stench of cigarettes fills the air. It seems as if every other person in NYC is smoking. This graph has the power to change people's minds about smoking. It is people that people in my community will avoid smoking if they find out the way in which it correlates with household income.

raw_comment:
Good morning again, Graph Analyzers –

About an hour ago, I wrote about Correlation vs. Association.  We say there is a correlation between two variables if both are quantitative.  Otherwise, we say that there is an association between any two variables, but in this case, for a quantitative variable (household income) and a categorical variable (smoking).

Now, let’s talk about if having a lower household income CAUSES people to smoke.  Or, if alternatively, if smoking CAUSES one to have a lower household income.  Both of these are described here as cause-and-effect relationships.
In statistics, there can only be a cause-and-effect relationship if we perform an experiment.  We would need to randomly assign a large group of individuals to one of two groups: where all members of one group are assigned to smoke and all members of the other group are assigned to not to smoke.  We would collect income information from all members of each group for many years. Then we would compare the average income for each group. Given what we know about the harmfulness of smoking, such an experiment would be unethical. When an experiment cannot be conducted, we can use observational studies to learn about the relationship between variables like smoking and income.

The data represented in this graph comes from an observational study.  There is NO cause-and-effect, but rather an ASSOCIATION!

raw_comment:
I noticed that this graph is a bar graph that compares different incomes in a household, in relation to if they smoke "every day" or "some days". I also noticed that the less income that is made, the more likely the person is to smoke.
I wonder if this is because most people who make less income are more stressed; since although smoking is harmful, it is known to relieve stress for many. I also wonder if more people of less income are prone to develop more illness because of the smoking, or because of the inability to spend money to get better healthcare.
This impacts my community because many of the people surrounding me are of higher income; I wonder if that can be a reason as to why I do not see that many people smoking around. I also feel that my community does a good job in educating people on the harm of smoking. 
A headline for this graph could be
"The Less Income, the More Smoking"

Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the relationship between smoking and household income in the United States.  The data comes from a survey by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).   

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the link to the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Keep noticing and wondering.  The next graphs on Covid herd immunity will be released before Friday, March 5 with moderation on Wednesday, March 10.

sentence_classifications.image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Horizontal bar chart.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Single-panel chart  
- Bars are arranged vertically by income category  
- No faceting, no stacking, no small multiples

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Household income category (<$35k, $35k–75k, $75k–$100k, >$100k) | Ordinal / categorical | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Share who smoke “every day” or “some days” (percent) | Quantitative | Bar length / horizontal position; numeric labels at bar ends |
| Highlighted income group (<$35k) | Categorical emphasis | Color/hue (yellow vs. gray) |

Additional visible text:
- The chart title states the measured outcome: **smokes “every day” or “some days”**
- Numeric values shown on bars: **21%, 15, 13, 7**

I wonder why cigarettes are not that popular in the US. I live in switzerland teenagers by the age of 13 start to smoke already and getting cigs is not very hard. I wonder if this is why the poor househole tends to smoke more because of this culture of the streets and the whole gang life. I wonder how this graph would look like when the question wouldnt be asking how much people smoke cigarettes but how much weed they smoke, i think the graph would look so different. I wonder what struggles the 21 percent go through since they smoke every day, and dont have a great income take care of others in their household.

raw_comment: I have noticed that the majority of people that smoke makes less money than the people who don't smoke. In the graph, more than 21% of Americans smoke per day, and more than half of household owners make less than 35,000 dollars. I am wondering if it is due to the amount of poverty in an environment or the location of where someone lives that impacts a person's behavior. The impact that this graph has on me and my community are that it is showing me the health risk of smoking and how much less a person makes when they do smoke. The graph is trying to inform people of the correlation between a person who smokes and the amount of money they make. This is to make more people aware of the downsides to smoking and getting them to quit so they can make more money for themselves. If I had to write a catchy headline I would say "the more you smoke the more money you lose."

A wonder how smoking effects ones ability to perform at a job. How does smoking effect ones cognitive ability? How much of this money that smokers actually make is spent on cigarettes and medical treatment to treat issues related to smoking?

This effects my community because smoking is clearly a serious health concern, but it's interesting to see how it could also effect one's work like and finances. I seriously hope the younger generations recognize the dangers of smoking and never smoke.

Smokers and Salaries

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the graph uses the color yellow to highlight the largest group, which is nearly 1/5 of the population of people who earn less than 35k. I notice that if you compare the poorest group and the richest group, you are 3 times as likely to smoke if you are poor than if you are rich. 

2. I wonder what this graph would look like if it was just "every day" smokers, and why it was chosen to display both the "every day" and "some days" categories. I wonder what this graph looks like for a more expensive vice like drinking or abuse of prescription medication. I wonder why they chose the color yellow. I wonder what this graph would look like if there were more income categories, like making >$300k. I also wonder what this looks like in different countries and comparing different factors like level of income or BMI, etc.

3. Because smoking is the cause of death for almost half a million people per year, the impact of this can be seen in the loved ones that are lost, and those that are impacted by this loss. 

4. "It Doesn't Pay to Smoke" would be my title for this graph

raw_comment: I notice that the lower the household income the more likely it is for there to be smokers. I see that for incomes less than 35K, there is about 21% more smokers. On the other hand, if we were to look at household incomes with at least 100K, then 7% would say that they smoke. I wonder as to why exactly it is that we see these results. Could it be that the less income a household makes, the more likely it is for that house to be located in a poor community and therefore be influenced by street culture. I would say that this impacts my  community very greatly because I come from a background that makes nowhere near 100K a year, and there is already a culture of smoking that happens with the adults in my life. Although this may be true, I do have faith that smoking will die down in my generation because most kids my age are already aware as to the dangers of smoking. raw_comment:
1. I notice that the percentage of adults who smoke “every day” or “some days” increases as household income decreases. For example, the percentage of adults who smoke that have a household income of less than $35k is 21% while the percentage of adults who smoke that have a household income of more than $100K is 7%. 
 
2. I wonder why this inverse relationship occurs. Does job insecurity among members of the American lower class cause civilians to smoke as means to relieve stress? Do tobacco companies specifically target lower income communities as areas to display cigarette advertisements? Or is there some other factor that results in this trend?
 
3. This has an impact on my community because low income neighborhoods in this area may be suffering from a smoking epidemic. If so, it is important that awareness about the consequences of smoking and resources on how to quit are spread throughout these areas. 
 
4. This graph shows the inverse relationship between household income and the percentage of smoking citizens.

raw_comment:
We notice that the graph suggests that as household income decreases, the number of smokers increases. / As income increases, the amount of people smoking decreases.

We wonder why people that are payed less smoke more. We wonder if this graph is only about cigarettes/nicotine or if it also included other substances that can be smoked like marijuana. We wonder if this graph would show the same trend if the data was for alcohol or other drugs. We wonder the ages of the respondents because 35K could be college students.  We wonder how this connects to education about smoking. We wonder how many people were surveyed and from what part of the world/country? We wonder why/are surprised that people who have more money to smoke do not spend their money on smoking. 

This has an impact on us and our community because based on the makeup of the community in terms of household income, we could be more or less exposed to second hand smoke. This information could help our community by informing targeted educational programs and advertisements about the dangers of smoking. This also suggests that communities where there are not as many high paying jobs, maybe because of quality of education, would be more effected by smoking overall.

raw_comment:
This graph shows the relationship between smoking and household income.
What do you notice?
- I notice that lower-income households tend to smoke more than higher-income households. It does show us that there are still people that smoke at higher levels of income, but this is most likely for leisure. People at these lower incomes are most likely smoking for stress relief.
What do you wonder?
-I wonder how much those people actually smoke, I wish they included a daily or weekly amount instead of just the "every day" or "some days" which is extremely general. I also wonder how much money/ how much of their income is going to buying cigarettes, etc. because that is taking valuable money away from necessities.
What impact does this have on you and your community?
-It doesn't have much impact on me or my community (unless that member of the community smokes). However, it does raise the question about why this correlation exists in the first place. Are people in lower-income brackets being targeted by cigarette companies? That would have an effect on my community because those people could be targeted for advertising.
Catchy headline?
Smoking and income.

What do you wonder? Why are we still positively advertising an item with negative effects?

Well what happens if an authority figure like a parent or employee (who was born in like the 50s/60s /70s /80s when smoking was cool) is supposed to be your role model but you follow them down the path of addiction? Then theres less adults who are good role models for kids, more cheating/affairs/ family disruption, more hospital time, hard times economically, and physical harm or even death.

What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea. “Smoke and fire, a horrible desire.”

raw_comment:
I noticed that those who make less based on household income smoke more. 
I also noticed that over half of the population in the United States smokes. Approximately 35-$75k and $75k-$100k account for about the same percentages, 15%, but $100,000 is significantly lower, around 7%. 
What do you wonder?

I wonder if those below $10k is lower than those between $10k and $35k. If the graph were to increment by 10k I wonder which would be highest. 

I wonder the percentage of vape/juul being used compared to cigarettes/cigars and which age has the highest percentage. 

I also wonder if there is a particular region in the United States that accounts for the highest percentage. 

Also I wonder if there are significantly more people in the below $35k compared to the other incomes, because that would make a large difference. 

Community

Those who make less have a greater susceptibility to smoking, in my community I don't believe there are more people who make less than 35k compared to those who make 35k-75k. This would suggest though, that if my community did typically make less than 35k then many more people would potentially be hospitalized for lung cancers, other types of cancers, second-hand smoke and air quality might not be as good. This would also tell me that maybe there needs to be a greater push for educating those on the risk of smoking.
